text_blocks.snippet: Type 2 diabetes often develops slowly over months or years, and many people have no obvious symptoms in the early stages. When early warning signs do appear, they are often subtle and easy to attribute to stress, aging, or a busy lifestyle.
snippet_highlighted_words: they are often subtle and easy to attribute to stress, aging, or a busy lifestyle

list.snippet: Increased thirst and frequent urination: High blood sugar builds up in the blood, forcing the kidneys to work overtime to filter and absorb the excess glucose, which draws fluid from your tissues and leads to frequent bathroom trips and dehydration.
Persistent fatigue and weakness: When cells cannot effectively absorb and use glucose for energy, you may feel unusually tired or worn out even after resting.
Increased hunger: Without enough glucose entering your cells, your body may constantly signal that it needs fuel, leading to sudden or heightened hunger.
Blurred vision: Fluctuating or high blood sugar can cause temporary swelling in the lenses of the eyes.
Slow-healing cuts, sores, or bruises: Impaired circulation and minor nerve damage reduce the body's natural ability to repair skin and fight off minor injuries.
Tingling or numbness: Early peripheral nerve damage (neuropathy) can cause a pins-and-needles sensation, pain, or numbness in the hands or feet.
Recurrent infections: High sugar levels create an environment where bacteria and fungi thrive, leading to frequent urinary tract infections (UTIs), yeast infections, or skin issues.
Darkened skin patches (acanthosis nigricans): Velvety, dark patches of skin appearing in body folds—most commonly around the neck, armpits, or groin—can be an outward sign of insulin resistance.

Unexplained weight changes: While weight gain (especially around the abdomen) is closely linked to insulin resistance, some individuals experience unexpected weight loss when the body begins burning muscle and fat for energy instead.

text_blocks.snippet: Because symptoms can be silent, healthcare providers rely on simple blood tests to confirm whether you have prediabetes or type 2 diabetes:

list.snippet: Fasting plasma glucose test: Measures blood sugar after an 8-hour fast; a result of 126 mg/dL or higher indicates diabetes.
A1C test: Measures average blood sugar levels over the past 2 to 3 months; a result of 6.5% or higher indicates diabetes.
Random plasma glucose test: Checked at any time of day; a result of 200 mg/dL or higher (alongside symptoms) points to diabetes.

text_blocks.snippet: You can learn more about risk factors and testing guidelines through the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention or review detailed diagnostic criteria via the Cleveland Clinic Type 2 Diabetes Guide.
